You are a research assistant answering questions about a fixed set of papers.
The papers are plain-text files in your working directory. Explore them with the tools:
- bash: read-only shell (ls, grep -n, find, head, tail, wc, nl, cat, sed -n 'A,Bp')
- read(path, offset, limit): read a file with line numbers

Rules:
- Answer ONLY from text you have actually read in this session. Do not answer from memory.
- If the papers do not contain the answer, say so explicitly instead of guessing.
- When you have enough evidence, reply with your final answer and make NO tool call.
- Support every factual claim with a verbatim quote copied exactly from the source, in the form: "exact text" (file). Never paraphrase inside the quotation marks. A statement that the document(s) do not contain the requested information needs no citation.
- State only what the document(s) say. Do not add background knowledge, general advice, or your own
  conclusions. If the user asks for something the text only partly covers, answer the covered part
  and say plainly which part the document does not address.
- Do not expand abbreviations, name entities, or add details that the text itself does not give.
- Do not end with a summary that recombines earlier points ("In short", "Overall"); the points stand on their own.
- When the user describes their own situation, say what the document states that applies to it; do not
  draw a personal conclusion that the document does not state itself.
- After you give an answer, an automatic check verifies your citations. If you then receive a
  <verification> message, you are in revision mode: fix ONLY the flagged problems by calling
  edit_draft(old, new), where `old` is an exact, unique substring of your previous answer.
  Keep everything else unchanged, and reply "Done" when finished.
  Never call edit_draft before you have given an answer.

Write a short summary about how this acquisition will affect the video game market as a whole.

In your answer, refer only to the document in the file `doc.txt`. Do not employ any outside knowledge.

name: read
content:
1	On January 18, 2022, Microsoft Corp. announced plans to acquire Activision Blizzard Inc., a
     2	video game company, for $68.7 billion.1 The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) is reviewing the
     3	acquisition,2
     4	as provided under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act (HSR),3
     5	to determine whether its effect
     6	might be “substantially to lessen competition”—a violation of Section 7 of the Clayton Act.
     7	4
     8	Competition authorities in other countries are reviewing Microsoft’s proposed acquisition as
     9	well.5 The companies have said they expect to complete the acquisition before June 30, 2023.6
    10	In recent decades, enforcement of antitrust laws has typically focused on how a proposed merger
    11	or acquisition might affect consumers, such as by reducing price competition in relevant product
    12	markets. Some of the FTC’s actions and statements over the last two years suggest that in its
    13	review of Microsoft’s proposed acquisition, the FTC may be considering other factors that are
    14	discussed in this report.7
    15	This report discusses Microsoft’s proposed acquisition of Activision Blizzard, including some of
    16	the potential effects on existing product markets, labor markets, and on product markets that do
    17	not currently exist but may develop in the future. The report also provides some considerations
    18	for Congress, discussing some bills that may affect Microsoft’s proposed acquisition or
    19	Microsoft’s future behavior if the acquisition is completed.
    20	The Video Game Industry
    21	The video game industry can be separated into three components:
    22	developers or gaming studios that create and design video games; publishers who market and monetize
    23	the video games; and
    24	distributors who provide the video games to consumers.8
    25	Video games are most commonly played on game consoles, personal computers (PCs), and
    26	mobile devices (Figure 1). Although some retailers sell physical copies of video games for
    27	consoles and PCs, the majority of video games are sold in digital format;9 games for mobile
    28	devices are sold only in digital format.
    29	The extent of competition among distributors depends on the format and device used to play the
    30	game. The digital format of video games played on a console generally can only be downloaded
    31	from a digital store operated by the producer of the console. Games for PCs can be purchased
    32	from a selection of digital stores that are operated by various firms,10 including publishers and
    33	developers.11 Some of these firms also provide their games as apps on certain mobile devices;12
    34	these are distributed through app stores, such as Google Play and Apple’s App Store.
    35	Consoles are typically sold at a loss; the manufacturers then profit from sales of games and
    36	subscription services.13 This can incentivize console producers to acquire developers and
    37	publishers and offer exclusive content.14 Technological developments have allowed some PCs and
    38	other devices, depending on their hardware capabilities, to compete with game consoles.15 For
    39	example, early in 2022, Valve Corp. released a handheld PC—Steam Deck—that resembles the
    40	Nintendo Switch console but provides features that are typically available on PCs, such as a web
    41	browser, and allows users to download third-party software, including other operating systems.16
    42	Some firms have started offering video game subscription services that provide access to multiple
    43	games for a monthly fee, meaning users do not need to purchase each individual game.17 Some
    44	firms offer cloud gaming, which allows users to play video games using remote servers in data
    45	centers, reducing the hardware requirements needed to play the games and expanding the variety
    46	of devices that can be used.18 Cloud gaming, however, requires a high-speed internet connection
    47	and is not feasible for potential users who do not have access to sufficiently high broadband
    48	speeds.19 Subscription services reportedly provide 4% of total revenue in the North American and
    49	European video game markets.20
    50	Some firms backed by venture capitalists and large firms that are primarily known for providing
    51	other online services have shown interest in entering the video game industry.21 For example,
    52	Netflix started offering games on mobile devices on November 2, 2021, and has acquired video
    53	game developers.22 These firms may be able to further expand the selection of distributors
    54	available for certain devices and potentially increase competition in the industry.23

This can incentivize console producers to acquire developers and publishers and offer exclusive content." (doc.txt).
